publications.title: The Influence of Financial News Sentiment on Investor Behavior and Market Dynamics: A Machine Learning Approach to Sentiment Classification
publications.subtitle: Zenodo
publications.description: Financial news sentiment influences investor decisions, but most research focuses on market-level outcomes rather than how individual investors with different personalities interpret the same news. We combined a Random Forest sentiment classifier (80.2% accuracy on FinancialPhraseBank) with a multi-agent simulation using FinBERT on 2,263 expert-labeled headlines, producing 226,300 decisions across 100 agents with randomized perception, portfolio memory, and herding dynamics. The clearest result was about neutral headlines: agents agreed on only 89.4% of neutral headlines compared to 98-99% for positive and negative, which mirrors the classifier's 26% neutral error rate. Herding cascades appeared in 32.8% (buy) and 16.0% (sell) of headlines, but ablation tests showed cascades barely changed when the herding mechanism was turned off, meaning agents were independently reaching the same conclusion rather than copying each other. A small shift toward caution appeared but was too small to be meaningful. Overall, neutral sentiment appears to be where both classification and investor agreement break down.

Eureka! After not submitting a project last year, I decided to run it back. This time with an actual team, Michael Mazilu , Rupert Kahng , and Julian Darou-Santos . We built an agentic execution layer that cuts token waste by semantically embedding ALL company data, so agents retrieve only what they need instead of scanning entire repos. Watches your Jira board, pulls context from GitHub, executes the work, opens PRs, and posts everything back automatically. With requiring human approval for dangerous actions, full observability and native integrations with Slack, GitHub, and Jira out of the box. Check the project out here!: https://lnkd.in/e5tXiKxa Unfortunately, in the end, we didn't get the dub. GG try next, daylight robbery. Onto the next! Thanks to my team and everyone else who came out( Adam Issa , Jacob John , Abdelrahman Eletr , Ibrahim Asif Qayyum , Divye Rawat , John Mannully , Jacob Blais , David Chen , Jerry Huang , also Nathan Yan who was here in spirit) that made this event even more fun.

FinNova Hacks What started as a vision to host a big hackathon turned out to be something smaller, but that doesn’t take away from how great the event was. Back in August, Jaitra Bhatt and I had the idea to run our own hackathon. We wanted to do something different, with live updates, constant changes, and more. We built a team and got to work. Over time, the team became less responsive, and it eventually came down to just the two of us again. But we didn’t let that stop us. We kept going. We got sponsors, found a venue, arranged food, and handled everything ourselves. And yesterday, it all came together. We weren’t able to run the full 48-hour, two-day hackathon we originally planned, but we still made it work. We turned it into a fast-paced case competition and hackathon-style event. FinNova Hacks happened, and that’s what matters. Grateful to everyone who supported us and showed up. This is just the first. Special thanks to Mohit Bhabak , Aadit Gupta , and Poneesh Kumar for hosting their workshops and judging! And @Manoj Kumar for being a guest speaker! Congrats to the winners, saanvi kumar and Pal Patel #hackathon #coding #casecompetition #team #technology #finance #fintech #FinNovaHacks

Hack Canada, what a weekend I usually participate in hackathons quite a bit, but this time I wanted to see what the other side looked like, organizing one. Last summer, I reached out to James Cao and the team to get involved. Shortly after, I interviewed and was accepted onto the team. Fast-forwarding to now, and here I am after the event, still in one piece. It was really cool seeing everything come together after months of planning and watching everyone build, learn, and work on their projects throughout the weekend. Without further ado, here is a quick summary of the weekend: Day 1: Lowkey arrived an hour after the opening ceremony and walked in to be met with a crowd of people swarming the front desk. I go off to the side, get questioned if I'm even an organizer, but eventually everything settled down, and I got in. After checking out everything, I head towards the opening ceremony room to see what's going on, then got aired TWICE by James Cao and Yang Xue (but all good, they were supa locked in). After opening, I finally got my handshake with them. Met Jason Cameron in the flesh, what a guy. Met a lot of awesome hackers throughout the night. Huge shoutout to: David Chen , John Mannully , Adam Issa , Jacob John , Ibrahim Asif Qayyum , Nathan Yan , Abdelrahman Eletr , Aryan, and Sohum(idt I got ur linkedins mb.) Day 2: I realized I wasn't going to get any sleep, so I stacked chairs for an hour and a half at 4:00 am. Then picked up trash for another hour. Taking my 20-minute power nap, I went back down to help set up the sponsor bay, where I met Jay Stapleton and Mike O'Driscoll from Tailscale. It was amazing learning more about what Tailscale does! Then I experienced the CS major's future of flipping burgers during the lunch rush. Day 3: Couldn't get any sleep again, but it was the final stretch. Judging started, and a few issues arose( Faiz Mustansar 👀 ), but all was well in the end, and judging commenced. Met Ethan Breit , Kaivalya Gandhi , and Lucas Crupi , really cool people(your samosas came at last). Then judging ended and the results were announced, 6 finalists and a lot of controversy. Apparently, a project that goes by RizzRank slipped through, which caused outrage. As an org, I felt like Captain America in that one image where he's hiding in that one comic, if anyone knows what I'm talking about. Thankfully, everything cooled off, and the closing ceremony came around. Congrats to all the winners, and thank you to all my fellow organizers who came together to make this event possible. Overall, organizing gave me a completely new appreciation for the amount of work that goes into events like this. It was also really interesting seeing all the different projects and hacker archetypes from the organizer’s perspective. Already excited for the next one.

A reminder that if you are a researcher and you tell me that you want to join this company because you don’t have compute to achieve your dreams, two things: - its probably true. being GPU poor is a very real thing. BUT - If I look at your GitHub or portfolio and there is no evidence of even trying to fine tune your own model or even any sort of attempt at self actualization then it comes off as you just want our compute and resources to run your own experiments and have zero desire to actually join our company to help us achieve our goals. We are not that kind of lab. I will reject or ghost you immediately We are not a stepping stone to get into a big lab, and we are definitely not in the business of just handing out compute to people just because they want to do their own thing. We are many researchers final destination, and we refuse to hire researchers from top labs every day. Try getting into a big lab first, there are a lot of people like you there. There are ways to learn and build meaningful things without needing compute of our scale. Use Claude or chat to tell you what those things are. Try it first THEN talk to me Last gentle reminder is you should assume that if you apply and don’t feel at least somewhat passionate about anime, and even just a little bit helps, just assume it’s not going to work out. I don’t know what people expect from me if I ask if you like anime and they shrug and say “not really”. Please don’t waste my time

Proud to share that our team placed in the Top 12 internationally out of 300+ teams in the NSRI Summer Research Hackathon 2026, a 6-day international research competition. This was my first-ever research competition, and I couldn’t have asked for a better team to experience it with: Agam Narain and Aarav Akkula. Over six intense days, we developed DualSense, a conceptual dual-biomarker hydrogel wound dressing designed for the earlier detection of chronic wound infections. Our project combined pH and uric acid biosensors with an AND-logic fusion algorithm to explore a more specific and real-time approach to infection monitoring. The biggest lesson from NSRI wasn’t just the final ranking; it was the process. We faced multiple setbacks, questioned our assumptions, revised our models, and had moments where our project felt far from where we wanted it to be. What made the difference was learning how to take feedback seriously, iterate quickly, and improve under pressure. Every round of critique helped us sharpen both our research and our presentation, and we came out of the competition much stronger than we entered it. For a first research competition, finishing among the top teams internationally is something I’m incredibly grateful for. More importantly, it gave me a real appreciation for research, engineering, collaboration, and the value of resilience when things don’t go according to plan. A huge thank you to the NSRI organizers, mentors, and judges for the opportunity and feedback throughout the competition. Excited to keep building, researching, and learning. #NSRI #Research #Engineering #Biotechnology #Innovation #Healthcare #STEM #HighSchoolResearch #Teamwork #Learning
